newsitem.title: ITALY: Bossi launches Italian secession drive.
newsitem.headline: Bossi launches Italian secession drive.

text.p: Separatist Umberto Bossi, sombre-faced and wearing a ribbon as a symbol of birth, launched a three-day march along Italy's River Po on Friday to declare "independence" for his would-be northern republic.

With a show of symbolism that could have been scripted in Hollywood, the Northern League leader solemnly filled a Venetian glass flask with water from the Alpine source of Italy's longest river and told supporters they were making history.

"We are on the verge of a historical act...the great battle for the liberation of Padania," Bossi later told a few hundred supporters at a nearby rally. Padania is the name of the self-styled state he vows to split from Italy within a year.
The League's "March to the Sea", which is expected to be met by counter-demonstrations of Italian unity, is due to culminate with a declaration of independence in Venice on Sunday evening.
Bossi, a keen self-publicist, has given short shrift to the notion that most Italians actually oppose his drive to create a state that lacks any separate linguistic or cultural identity.
A poll by Datamedia published on Friday found that only 7.6 percent were in favour of secession, with 85.6 percent opposed.

Seeking to dramatise the first of a weekend of events that he hopes will draw one million followers of his breakaway dream, the League leader had intended to swoop by helicopter to Pian del Re, a mountain plateau 2,040 metre (6,690 feet) up in the far west of Italy near the border with France.
But high winds forced him to land nearby and continue by car to where about 200 people, mostly from the media, had gathered to watch the ceremony.

Bossi, dressed in a casual cardigan and sporting a bright pink ribbon echoing the ribbons Italians pin to their front doors to celebrate the birth of a child, was flanked by police and green-shirted stewards from his own security detachment.
Looking solemn, he filled the flask and placed it in a green box. Behind him, supporters carried a banner declaring "Padania is born at the Po".

Opposition to Bossi's trip has been vocal right across the political spectrum, where all sides say federal reform is the way to tackle popular frustration with high taxes, bureacracy and public sector inefficiency in Italy's richest region.

Irene Pivetti, the former speaker of the lower house of parliament whom Bossi summarily expelled from the party on Thursday for preferring a federal Italy rather than full independence for the north, said Bossi's tactics nauseated her.

The Roman Catholic Church said it was concerned and Prime Minister Romano Prodi, whose centre-left government is committed to federalism, said Bossi's project had "no roots in the past and no future".
Three porn stars even staged their own full frontal attack on the campaign. One paraded stark naked in front of parliament in body paint in the red, white and green of the Italian flag.
Condemnation also came from former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, whose stormy seven-month coalition with Bossi's League in 1994 ended in the fall of his government.
Berlusconi expressed understanding for northern discontent but declared secession a non-starter that sowed "ethnic hatred".
Bossi, whose party flag bears the symbol of a knight with a sword, was undeterred.

With the rallying cry "All for one and one for all", he urged supporters who cheered him with cries of "Bossi, Bossi" and "Freedom, freedom" to take photographs of the occasion as a souvenir of the birth of their nation.
